topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Calculate Digits of Pi

outline.topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Colliding Blocks Calculate Digits of Pi

sections.title: The Hook: The Bouncing Blocks Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: Two blocks of mass M and m (where m = M × 100^n) slide on a frictionless surface towards a wall. How many collisions occur until they stop moving toward the wall?
sections.example: Visual: A small block 'm' between a wall and a massive block 'M'. As 'M' gets exponentially heavier, the number of 'clinks' grows: 3, 31, 314, 3141... mimicking digits of π.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Elastic Collisions and Conservation
sections.content: Briefly review the conservation of momentum and kinetic energy in perfectly elastic collisions. Explain that for two objects of equal mass, they simply exchange velocities (acting like they passed through each other).
sections.example: Visual: Two balls of equal mass collide and 'swap' velocities; animation shows them as ghost-like passing through each other to simplify trajectory calculations.

sections.title: Mapping Physics to Geometry
sections.content: Explain the 'Unfolding' technique. Convert the 1D collision problem into the motion of a single particle in a 2D plane reflecting off the walls of a 'wedge' shaped potential barrier.
sections.example: Visual: A graph where the x-axis is the velocity of block m and the y-axis is the velocity of block M. A collision is a line segment reflecting off a diagonal boundary line.

sections.title: The Emergence of Pi
sections.content: Demonstrate that the total number of reflections is determined by the angle of the wedge. As the mass ratio approaches infinity, the angle of the wedge approaches zero, effectively 'trapping' the motion on the arc of a circle.
sections.example: Visual: The path of the particle traces an arc of a circle. The number of reflections corresponds to how many times the path hits the 'wall' boundaries, which is geometrically related to π/θ.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap how a discrete mechanical system (collisions) maps onto a continuous geometric constant (pi). Emphasize that math is hidden in the most unexpected physical interactions.
sections.example: Visual: A final animation showing the block ratio 1:1,000,000 resulting in exactly 3,141 collisions, closing with the statement: 'Physics is the language of geometry'.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Bouncing Blocks Paradox
lecture_lines: Two blocks slide toward a wall.
A small block sits between wall and massive block.
Exponentially heavier blocks create more collisions.
Collisions count the digits of Pi.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Elastic Collisions and Conservation
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions conserve momentum and kinetic energy.
Equal masses simply exchange velocities upon impact.
Treat them as passing through each other.
animations: Display momentum formula p = mv in center (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Mapping Physics to Geometry
lecture_lines: Velocity vectors form a 2D particle plane.
Reflections hit a potential barrier wedge.
animations: Draw a 2D plane with two axes labeled x1 and x2.
Plot a diagonal line representing the conservation of energy.
Animate a point moving along this line as blocks bounce.

storyboard.title: The Emergence of Pi
lecture_lines: Number of reflections depends on wedge angle.
Mass ratio makes the angle approach zero.
The particle traces a circle arc path.
Reflections define the ratio related to Pi.
Geometric limits reveal the hidden constant.
animations: Animate the point spiraling near the axes origin.
Overlay the digits of pi emerging near the trajectory.
Highlight the final crossing point of the trajectory.

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Discrete collisions map to continuous geometry.
Mathematics emerges from simple physical systems.
Physics is the language of geometry.
animations: Display the final ratio of collision counts.
Fade out all elements to black.
